name: Japanese
notes: Start with hiragana — it is a true alphabet of 46 sounds and can be learned in a week. Once you can read it, everything else in Japanese becomes approachable. Japanese has no tones and very regular pronunciation, which makes speaking it far easier than reading it.
syllabus: Both kana in full, 110 kanji (the whole JLPT N5 kanji list), and about 450 words and phrases — a little over half of N5 vocabulary (roughly 800 words). N5 is the first of five official levels; passing it means simple, slow conversations. Grammar is in the sentence-patterns deck and the guide. What is still missing: the rest of the N5 words, and audio.
